shots.narration: In one African crater,
more than eight in ten of the meals lions were seen eating had been killed by hyenas.
By the end, Doug hides behind lions, and the lions leave.
Dusk.
The Lie.
Hyenas are famous for living on other animals' kills,
but in Kenya's Masai Mara, researchers found that spotted hyenas kill about ninety-five percent of the food they eat.
If you ate three meals a day for a week,
that would be twenty meals you cooked yourself and a single takeaway.
For decades, the accepted picture was simple:
lions did the hunting, and hyenas hung around the edges and stole.
Then, in Tanzania, a biologist named Hans Kruuk started watching what hyenas actually did at night.
Here's where the picture flips.
Kruuk kept finding the same scene, in which the hyenas had made the kill
and the lions had strolled in afterwards and chased them off.
In the Ngorongoro Crater, where hyenas outnumbered lions about ten to one,
it was usually the lions eating hyena kills.
The thief in the famous picture was the lion.
The narrator has used this chalkboard before.
Every tick is the narrator's call, not a study.
Tonight's question is which one is worse to be near, on foot, until dawn.
Doug did not agree to this.
Doug has brought a plate of leftovers for the scavengers,
and sat down beside it to watch.
The hyenas walk straight past it.
Doug has died. Again.
Nobody touched the leftovers, because hyenas prefer to start from scratch,
and they have the teeth to finish anything.
The Bite.
A spotted hyena doesn't just eat the meat off a skeleton.
It eats the skeleton.
Its heavy cheek teeth can crush large bones,
and at a carcass a hyena will swallow the meat, the bone and even the hair.
When scientists measured the bite of one captive hyena,
it reached about four thousand five hundred newtons, and hyenas in the wild probably bite even harder.
That's roughly the weight of six grown men, all squeezed into one set of jaws.
Then the bone gets digested,
and hyena droppings come out white because they carry the minerals from all that bone.
One study found between one thousand and twenty thousand times more calcium and phosphorus in them than in the soil around them.
Here's the difference.
When lions are around a carcass, hyenas often just wait for them to abandon it,
then come back later for whatever remains.
The lion eats the meal.
The hyena eats the plate it came on.
Doug has brought the hyena a gift, a chew bone from a pet shop, with a bow on it.
The hyena takes his walking stick instead,
and bites it cleanly in half.
Doug has died.
The hyena turned down the leftovers and the gift, and broke the stick.
Doug decided to run before it got round to the cap.
The Chase.
A lion that misses on its first rush usually gives up,
but a hyena that misses just keeps on running.
Lions hunt by stalking and seldom charge until they're within about thirty meters,
and they can't hold that pace for more than a hundred to two hundred meters.
Even then, a lion hunting alone by day succeeds less than one time in five.
Hyenas work differently, and Hans Kruuk watched them run down adult wildebeest in chases of about five kilometers,
at speeds of up to sixty kilometers an hour.
In the Kalahari Desert, a typical hyena chase ran from half a kilometer to two and a half.
Five kilometers is a whole park run,
while the lion's limit is half a lap of a running track.
Over the first sprint they're both fast, so the lion gets a tick, for honesty.
The worst part is the plan.
Against a lion, the plan is "don't be close."
Against a hyena, the plan is "don't get tired."
Doug is always tired.
Doug has outrun the lion, at least in his head,
and at two hundred meters he stops to catch his breath and look back at the empty grass behind him.
Doug has died. Again.
The cap kept rolling for a while,
and then, somewhere out in the dark, something started laughing.
The Laugh.
A hyena's laugh isn't laughter.
It's the sound of a hyena under stress,
and it tells everyone listening how old it is and where it ranks.
Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, recorded hundreds of giggles from captive hyenas
and found that the pitch drops as a hyena gets older.
Dominant hyenas giggle in a steady, confident way,
while low-ranking ones sound more variable, and each animal even has its own voice.
They giggle in tense moments, like a squabble over food
or when lions chase them off a kill,
and the researchers think the wobble in the call carries frustration.
But the giggle is not the sound to worry about.
That's the whoop, a long-range call that hyenas use to recruit the rest of the clan,
and it carries up to about five kilometers.
That's nearly fifty soccer fields laid end to end.
Doug laughs back, to be friendly,
and the giggling gets louder and higher
until one low-ranking hyena backs off, frustrated, and leaves.
Doug is fine.
He has no idea what he said to it,
and the narrator, watching from a safe distance, had hoped for a different result.
The hyena that left was whooping now,
and that is the call that brings the others.
Midnight.
The Clan.
At rich sites like the Masai Mara and the Ngorongoro Crater,
a single hyena clan can reach around a hundred and thirty animals.
A hundred and thirty hyenas wouldn't fit on a school bus rated for seventy-two passengers,
so they would need two.
Every one of them has a rank, and the rank is inherited,
so young hyenas take their place in the order from their mother.
Females outrank all the males,
and to bring down big prey, a clan hunts in groups of roughly eight to twenty-five.
Now do the arithmetic.
In the Ngorongoro Crater, up to five hundred and fifty hyenas share the crater floor with just twenty-five to forty adult lions.
A lion pride is a family,
but a hyena clan is a town,
and it has strict rules about who gets to eat first.
Prides are groups too, so the lion gets its last tick.
The last hyena Doug met was the size of a lion.
This one is smaller.
That did not help.
Doug counts the eyes in his torch beam,
gets to twelve, and gives up.
Doug has died. Again.
The clan sat down to eat, and the narrator went to fetch a stopwatch.
The Stomach.
Thirty-five hyenas can finish an entire adult zebra in thirty-six minutes.
Hans Kruuk also watched the remains of a hundred-kilogram young wildebeest disappear in less than fifteen minutes.
A single hyena can eat at least fourteen and a half kilograms of meat in one meal,
which for a small adult is more than a third of its own body weight.
That's more than a hundred and twenty quarter-pound burgers, eaten in one sitting.
At a carcass, hyenas compete mostly by eating faster, not by fighting the way lions do,
and a low-ranking male has to gorge quickly before the females push him aside.
And that's where Doug's plan falls apart, because there is no "come back for it later."
Nothing is left to come back for.
Water doesn't stop them either,
because hyenas have been seen diving under floating carcasses to take a bite, staying under for up to twelve seconds.
Doug has hidden his packed lunch in the water hole, on a string, for later,
and the hyena goes in after it first.
Doug has died. Again.
Doug wanted somewhere with people in it,
and the narrator knew a city where the hyenas come in for dinner.
Before dawn.
The Town.
The old walled city of Harar, in Ethiopia, has holes in its wall for hyenas.
Sixteen of them.
Spotted hyenas have roamed Harar's streets for at least five hundred years,
coming and going through those openings and cleaning up the city's scraps.
The old town, Harar Jugol, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site covering forty-eight hectares,
about the size of Vatican City, the smallest country in the world.
In the evenings, men known as the hyena men feed wild hyenas by hand.
Each year, people there also set out porridge for the hyenas,
in a ritual believed to keep anyone from being attacked in the year ahead.
Further north, around the city of Mekelle, hyenas mostly scavenge waste from butchers and households.
During the fifty-five-day fast before Easter, when Orthodox Christians stop eating meat,
researchers found donkey hair in more than twice as many of the hyenas' droppings.
The remarkable part is what all of this says about hyenas.
They notice where the food comes from and change with it,
and one city chose to deal with them by inviting them to dinner.
Doug walks into Harar at night and finds hyenas taking meat from a man's hand,
so he holds out a piece too.
It is taken, politely.
Doug is fine.
The narrator suspects it only worked because a professional was present,
and Doug walked back out of town to sleep.
The Sleepers.
Lions are the animal people fear in the dark,
but there are many records of spotted hyenas attacking people while they sleep.
Hyenas are usually shy around people,
and they can run from a person at up to three hundred meters, further than any other African carnivore.
That's roughly the height of the Eiffel Tower, laid on its side.
Even so, they can prey on people who are sleeping outdoors, and they sometimes break into huts and tents.
In one reserve in Mozambique, more than half of the recorded hyena attacks happened while people were sleeping in the open.
Here's who is actually out there in the dark.
Lions are what people picture,
but hyenas are the ones that come right into towns, and even into cities, to eat what people throw away.
Doug is sleeping outside because of the heat, on a mat, beside a hand-painted sign that says "Lions: no",
and in the night his torch rolls away.
Doug has died. Again.
The sign was right, and no lions came,
so for the last hour of the night, Doug went out to find some.
The Mob.
Hyenas can take a kill away from lions,
and in the Ngorongoro Crater they manage it when they bring in at least six times as many hyenas as there are lions.
Six to one is a full hockey team, goalie included, against a single player.
That's against lionesses and young males, though,
because when an adult male lion is there, the lions always keep the kill, however many hyenas show up.
This rivalry runs both ways,
and in the crater, lions are the main cause of death for hyenas.
Here's the honest part.
Lions are the bigger danger to people.
In Tanzania, lions killed more than five hundred and sixty people between nineteen ninety and two thousand four.
In villages beside the Serengeti, lions caused most of the reported attacks on people, ahead of leopards and hyenas.
But this scoreboard was never about people in general,
because it's about Doug, alone, on foot, all night.
A lion might be the worse animal to meet once,
but a hyena is the worse animal to be near for a whole night.
So, with dawn still an hour away, Doug hides behind a pride of lionesses on their kill,
because lions are the scary ones.
Then the whooping starts,
and the clan arrives out of the grey light,
and it outnumbers them by a lot.
The lions leave.
Doug does not.
Doug has died. Again.
The cap is heading to Harar,
where someone will feed it by hand.
Doug deaths: two hundred and sixty-seven.
Killed by lions: none.
The next place Doug isn't welcome is on your screen now.
